introduction-who-are-you-and-what-can-yo.core: Identity and access management splits into authentication (proving who you are: passwords, MFA, passkeys, certificates), authorisation (deciding what you may do: roles, attributes, policies), and federation (letting a trusted identity provider vouch for you across apps via OIDC or SAML). Centralising authentication in an IdP and expressing authorisation as clear policy reduces password sprawl, eases offboarding, and makes access auditable.

first_principles.problem: An employee leaves, but their accounts in 30 separate apps stay active for months.
truths: Many apps need one source of truth.

analogy.title: A passport and visa system
analogy.story: The passport (authentication) proves who you are; the visa (authorisation) says what you may do; trusted issuing countries (IdPs) are recognised abroad (federation).
analogy.breaks: Passports last years; tokens should last minutes to hours.

check.q: What's the difference between authentication and authorisation?
check.a: Authentication proves who you are; authorisation decides what you're allowed to do.

the-enterprise-classic-saml.core: SAML 2.0 is an XML-based federation standard from 2005. The user hits a service provider (SP), is redirected to the identity provider (IdP), authenticates, and the IdP posts back a digitally signed XML assertion with the subject, attributes such as email and groups, conditions and an expiry, which the SP validates against the IdP's certificate. It's ubiquitous in enterprise SaaS, but XML signature handling has caused serious vulnerabilities (signature wrapping), so use mature libraries.

first_principles.problem: An enterprise customer requires SSO via their corporate IdP, and the SaaS app only has username and password.
truths: Assertions must be trusted and verified.

analogy.title: A sealed letter of introduction
analogy.story: Your company writes a signed letter vouching for you; the partner checks the seal and the date before letting you in.
analogy.breaks: Letters are read by people; SAML assertions are parsed by code that can be tricked.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: SP validates and maps 'finance' group to role.

check.q: What must a service provider validate in a SAML assertion?
check.a: The IdP signature, audience, recipient, time conditions (NotBefore/NotOnOrAfter) and that it responds to its own request.

modern-auth-oauth-20-vs-openid-connect-o.core: OAuth 2.0 is an authorisation framework: it lets an app obtain access tokens to call APIs on a user's behalf, with scopes and consent, without handling their password. It doesn't define who the user is. OpenID Connect adds authentication on top: an ID token (a signed JWT with sub, iss, aud, exp and claims), a userinfo endpoint and discovery. Use OIDC for login and OAuth access tokens for API access. Don't use an ID token as an API token.

first_principles.problem: An app uses OAuth access tokens as proof of login, accepting tokens issued for other apps.

analogy.title: A valet key vs an ID card
analogy.story: OAuth gives a valet key (limited access to drive your car); OIDC adds an ID card proving who you are.
analogy.breaks: Valet keys are physical; tokens can be replayed if stolen.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: API checks aud = its own identifier.

check.q: Why shouldn't an API accept ID tokens as access tokens?
check.a: ID tokens are meant for the client app (their audience is the client), not for authorising API calls; accepting them breaks audience isolation.

oidc-in-action-tokens-and-flows.core: The recommended flow for web, mobile and SPA apps is Authorization Code with PKCE. The app redirects to the IdP with a code_challenge; the user authenticates; the IdP returns a short-lived code; the app exchanges the code plus code_verifier at the token endpoint for ID, access and refresh tokens. Machine-to-machine uses the client-credentials flow, and devices use the device-code flow. The implicit and password grants are deprecated. Store tokens safely (httpOnly cookies, a BFF pattern) and rotate refresh tokens.

first_principles.problem: A SPA uses the implicit flow and stores tokens in localStorage, exposing them to XSS.
truths: Codes are safer to pass via browser than tokens.
PKCE binds the code to the requester.
Browser storage is reachable by scripts.

analogy.title: A cloakroom ticket exchanged at the desk
analogy.story: The browser carries only a ticket (code); the desk (token endpoint) hands the coat (tokens) to whoever shows the matching stub (PKCE verifier).
analogy.breaks: Tickets are physical; codes must be single-use and short-lived.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Stolen codes useless without the verifier.

code.text:
1. verifier = random(43..128 chars); challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier))
2. GET /authorize?response_type=code&client_id=web&redirect_uri=...&scope=openid%20orders:read&code_challenge=<challenge>&code_challenge_method=S256&state=xyz&nonce=n1
3. IdP redirects: /callback?code=SplxlOBe&state=xyz
4. POST /token  grant_type=authorization_code&code=SplxlOBe&code_verifier=<verifier>&client_id=web
5. ← { id_token, access_token, refresh_token, expires_in: 600 }

check.a: Authorization code interception: a stolen code can't be exchanged without the original code_verifier.

controlling-access-rbac-role-based-acces.core: RBAC assigns permissions to roles (viewer, editor, admin, billing-manager) and roles to users or groups, so access is managed by membership rather than per-user grants. It's simple to understand and audit and maps well to job functions, as in Kubernetes RBAC and cloud IAM roles. Its weaknesses are role explosion when you need context such as 'only their own region's orders', and over-broad roles that accumulate permissions over time.

first_principles.problem: Every engineer has admin in production because creating granular roles felt too hard.
truths: Context isn't expressible in pure roles.

analogy.title: Job titles with keycard access
analogy.story: 'Cleaner' opens supply rooms, 'Manager' opens offices; new staff get the title's keycard.
analogy.breaks: Job titles are stable; cloud permissions multiply with every new service.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Team can deploy in its namespace only.

code.text:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata: { name: deployer, namespace: shop }
rules:
  - apiGroups: [apps]
    resources: [deployments]
    verbs: [get, list, update, patch]
---
kind: RoleBinding
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
metadata: { name: shop-deployers, namespace: shop }
subjects: [{ kind: Group, name: "oidc:team-shop", apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io }]
roleRef: { kind: Role, name: deployer, apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io }

check.a: Creating ever more specific roles to express contextual rules, leading to an unmanageable number of roles.

fine-grained-control-abac-attribute-base.core: ABAC decides access by evaluating policies over attributes of the subject (department, clearance, region), resource (owner, classification, tenant), action and environment (time, device posture, location). For example: allow if user.department == resource.department and resource.classification <= user.clearance. It's expressive and avoids role explosion, and is implemented with policy engines (OPA/Rego, Cedar, AWS IAM conditions and tags). The trade-off is that it's harder to audit 'who can access X' without tooling.

first_principles.problem: A multi-tenant SaaS needs users to see only their own tenant's data in their own region, which needs hundreds of roles in RBAC.
truths: Attributes already exist on users and data.

analogy.title: A bouncer checking several conditions
analogy.story: 'Over 18, on the guest list for tonight's event, and not wearing trainers' rather than a single VIP pass.
analogy.breaks: Bouncers can explain decisions; ABAC needs tooling to answer 'who has access'.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One policy covers every tenant and region.

check.q: What's ABAC's main advantage over RBAC?
check.a: It expresses contextual rules (tenant, region, time, device) with policies over attributes, avoiding role explosion.
